newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya presses ahead with sugar expansion plans.
newsitem.headline: Kenya presses ahead with sugar expansion plans.

text.p: Kenya is pressing ahead with plans to increase sugar production and has contracted 1,400 farmers around Busia, where a new factory is expected to be completed in 1998, the Kenya Sugar Authority (KSA) said.
"Our efforts are geared towards expanding the industry," the Authority said in a report. "The response is positive."
"Future prospects at bridging the supply and demand gap are indeed bright in the industry."
It posted production at 384,171 tonnes in 1995, from 303,292 in 1994, and forecasts a jump to 420,000 tonnes in 1996 on better weather and management.
Domestic demand had risen steadily to 560,000 tonnes this year, it added, noting that the rise had contrasted with production declines in 1992, 1993 and 1994, mainly through a lack of cash.
The report, passed to Reuters on Thursday, said new technology being introduced at Mumias Sugar Company, the main miller, would expand its crushing capacity to 8,000 from 7,000 tonnes per day.

It said that planning for the expansion of the debt-burdened Nzoia Sugar Company to a capacity of 6,200 tonnes from 3,000 per day was under way and included taking on board a strategic partner. It did not say whether such a partner had been found.
Kenya has six major mills, including Mumias and Nzoia. The seventh miller produces just 500 tonnes of sugar a year.

The mill in Busia, near the border with Uganda, is part of the process of privatising Mumias Sugar Company. Government officials suggest problems have arisen in initial funding for the project expected from Tate & Lyle Plc. The Mumias mill is managed by Booker Tate, a subsidiary of Tate & Lyle.

"We are ready for privatisation of the Mumias company. But the problem so far is that there are outstanding issues still to be thrashed out between the government and Tate & Lyle," said an official at the government privatisation unit.
The official would not say what the problems were.
Land under sugar cane in Kenya rose to 123,688 hectares in 1995 from 104,675 in 1994, the authority said.
The authority said its own problems included lack of adequate funding for rehabilitation and maintenance of existing facilities to improve their operational efficiency.
Others were lack of funding for cane development, drought in 1992/93, inadequate research and poor management.

But the authority said it had established a sugar development levy to fund research and rehabilitation and was restructuring the overall industry's institutional set-up to provide an enabling environment for better performance.
It was also strengthening agricultural extension services.
The authority said it required cane varieties that are early maturing, high yielding, high in sucrose content, drought tolerant and resistant to pests and disease to boost growth.
